bigPicture.subtitle: A Living Hope for Exiles
paragraphs: Picture small groups of believers scattered across the northern half of what is now Turkey — in harbour towns, mountain villages and Roman cities. A few years ago they worshipped idols, drank at the feasts of the guilds and lived like everyone around them. Then they heard about Jesus, were baptised and began to live differently. Now their neighbours call them strange. Their old friends slander them. Some husbands are angry with their believing wives; some masters beat their believing slaves. And rumours are coming from Rome that the emperor himself may turn against the Christians. They are at home in their own towns, yet suddenly they feel like foreigners.

To these people the apostle Peter writes a letter of hope. He calls them “the chosen ones who are living as foreigners in the Dispersion” (1 Peter 1:1). They have lost their place in the world, but they have gained something better: God “caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (1 Peter 1:3). Their home is not here. Their inheritance is kept in heaven. And their suffering is not a sign that God has forgotten them, but the path their Lord walked before them.

The letter's great theme is suffering followed by glory. Peter uses the language of suffering more than any other New Testament letter, and he always ties it to Christ: “For to this you were called, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his steps” (1 Peter 2:21). He calls believers to holy living, good conduct before unbelievers, humble submission, love for one another and courageous hope. He does not promise escape from the fire. He promises that the fire will prove their faith and end in glory.

The writer is Simon Peter, the fisherman Jesus called to be a fisher of men, the disciple who confessed “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16) and then denied Him three times. After the resurrection Jesus restored him with three questions and three commands to feed His sheep. In this letter the restored shepherd feeds the flock. He writes “Through Silvanus” (1 Peter 5:12) — Silas, Paul's travelling companion, who probably helped with the writing or carried the letter — from “Babylon” (1 Peter 5:13), most likely a code name for Rome. Church tradition says Peter was crucified there under Nero not long afterwards. When he tells suffering Christians to stand firm, he is preparing for his own martyrdom.

bridge.intro: James ended by pointing ahead to 1 Peter and 2 Peter. The two letters stand side by side among the letters written to the whole scattered church, and they share many themes — but where James tests faith by its works, Peter anchors faith in hope.

points.title: From ‘The Twelve Tribes in the Dispersion’ to ‘Foreigners in the Dispersion’
points.body: James wrote “to the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion” (James 1:1). Peter writes “to the chosen ones who are living as foreigners in the Dispersion” (1 Peter 1:1). Both use the same word, διασπορά, the scattering — a word that once described Israel in exile. Now it describes the whole church, Jewish and Gentile believers together, living as strangers in a world that is not their final home.

points.title: From Faith Proved by Testing to Faith Proved by Fire
points.body: James said, “knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance” (James 1:3). Peter uses the same word and adds the image: “that the proof of your faith, which is more precious than gold that perishes even though it is tested by fire, may be found to result in praise, glory, and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 1:7). Both begin their letters with joy in trials. James shows what trials produce now; Peter shows what they will produce when Christ appears.

points.title: From ‘Humble Yourselves’ to ‘Under the Mighty Hand of God’
points.body: Both apostles quote the same Proverb. James wrote, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6), and “Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you” (James 4:10). Peter writes, “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time” (1 Peter 5:6), and then, like James, moves straight to resisting the devil (1 Peter 5:8–9). The two letters agree that humility and spiritual warfare go together.

points.title: From Faith That Works to Good Works the World Can See
points.body: James insisted that faith must be shown by works. Peter turns those works towards a watching world: “having good behavior among the nations, so in that of which they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they see, glorify God in the day of visitation” (1 Peter 2:12). For Peter, a holy and gracious life is the church's answer to slander, and its most powerful witness.

coreTheme.title: Born Again to a Living Hope — Through Suffering to Glory
paragraphs: The letter opens with praise: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (1 Peter 1:3). That living hope is the anchor of everything Peter says. Because Jesus rose, believers have a new birth, an imperishable inheritance and a future glory, and their present sufferings are short and purposeful.

Peter never pretends that suffering is pleasant. He writes, “Beloved, don’t be astonished at the fiery trial which has come upon you, to test you, as though a strange thing happened to you” (1 Peter 4:12). “But because you are partakers of Christ’s sufferings, rejoice; that at the revelation of his glory you also may rejoice with exceeding joy” (1 Peter 4:13). The pattern is the pattern of Christ Himself — first the cross, then the crown. The prophets searched for it, “when he predicted the sufferings of Christ, and the glories that would follow them” (1 Peter 1:11).

The letter closes with a promise that gathers the whole theme: “But may the God of all grace, who called you to his eternal glory by Christ Jesus, after you have suffered a little while, perfect, establish, strengthen, and settle you” (1 Peter 5:10). Suffering is ‘a little while’; glory is ‘eternal’. The God who allows the fire is the God of all grace, and He will finish what He began.

Peter's theme runs through the whole New Testament. Paul wrote, “For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which will be revealed toward us” (Romans 8:18). Jesus told the disciples on the Emmaus road, “Didn’t the Christ have to suffer these things and to enter into his glory?” (Luke 24:26). And Peter, who once rebuked Jesus for speaking of the cross, now teaches the church to follow Him on the same road.

truths.intro: As we journey through these 5 chapters, the Holy Spirit wants to anchor these truths in your spirit:

items.title: Your Identity Is Secure
items.body: Before Peter tells believers how to live, he tells them who they are: chosen by the Father, set apart by the Spirit, sprinkled with the blood of Jesus (1:2); born again to a living hope (1:3); “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession” (1 Peter 2:9). The world may reject you, but God has chosen you. Your security does not depend on your circumstances.

items.title: Holiness and Good Conduct Are Your Witness
items.body: Peter calls believers to be holy because God is holy (1:15–16), to abstain from fleshly desires “which war against the soul” (1 Peter 2:11), and to live such good lives among unbelievers that slander is silenced. In marriage, at work and under authority, the believer's conduct is meant to point people to God. Your life is the first sermon most people will hear.

items.title: Suffering With Christ Leads to Glory With Christ
items.body: Peter does not explain away suffering. He shows that Christ suffered first — “Because Christ also suffered for sins once, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring you to God” (1 Peter 3:18) — and that believers who suffer for doing good share in His sufferings and will share in His glory. You can cast all your anxieties on Him, “because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7).

preparation.intro: Before we step into Chapter 1, prepare your spirit with these reflections:

items.title: Where Do You Feel Like a Foreigner?
items.body: Where has following Jesus made you feel out of place — at work, in your family, among old friends, in your culture? Peter will tell you that this feeling is not a mistake but a sign of who you are. Bring that place to God, and read this letter as His word to exiles.

items.title: What Fire Are You Facing?
items.body: Name the trial, pressure, criticism or suffering you are facing because of your faith or simply because life is hard. As you read 1 Peter, look for how God wants to use it to prove your faith and prepare you for glory — and for the living hope that can hold you while it lasts.

prayerOfActivation: “Blessed be You, God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to Your great mercy caused me to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus from the dead. As I open the first letter of Peter, I thank You that I am chosen, sprinkled with the blood of Jesus and kept by Your power for an inheritance that cannot fade. Where I feel like a foreigner in this world, remind me that my home is with You. Where I am facing fire, prove my faith and make it more precious than gold. Make me holy as You are holy. Let my good conduct silence slander and lead others to glorify You. Teach me to follow in the steps of Jesus, who suffered for me. Humble me under Your mighty hand, and help me cast all my anxieties on You, because You care for me. And when I have suffered a little while, perfect, establish, strengthen and settle me, as You have promised. Thank You that Peter, who once denied You, was restored to feed Your sheep. Feed me now through his words. In Jesus' name, Amen.”
